definition: A hallucination is when an AI gives you a wrong answer that sounds completely right — a made-up citation, a confident-but-wrong date, a product feature that doesn't exist. The model isn't lying to you. It's predicting plausible-sounding text, and plausible isn't the same as true.

edges.label: born from
edges.note: The model predicts the next plausible token — not the next true one.

edges.label: kept in check by
edges.note: Grounding answers in retrieved documents is the main practical defense.

example.body: A lawyer asked an AI for legal precedents to support his motion. It returned beautifully formatted case citations — names, courts, years, perfect Bluebook style. None of the cases existed. He filed them with the court anyway, and the judge was not amused. This really happened — and it's the shape of most hallucinations: flawless packaging, empty box.
example.title: The case law that never existed

footnotes.body: Hallucinations are intrinsic to the next-token-prediction objective: the model is trained to produce likely text, with no built-in fact checker. Mitigations include retrieval grounding (RAG), asking for citations that can be verified, lower temperature settings, and verification loops where a second pass checks claims against sources.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: Hallucination
tagline: When the AI states something false with total confidence.
whyItMatters: This is the failure mode that matters most in day-to-day use. The answers that are wrong *and* confident are the ones that slip past busy people. Once you accept that hallucinations are normal behavior — not rare glitches — you start verifying anything that matters, which is exactly the right instinct.
